hook.text: Stare at a red square for 30 seconds, then look at white paper. You'll see a green ghost. That's an afterimage.

buildup.text: Afterimages form because cone cells fatigue. Stare at red long enough and the red cones exhaust their response.

discovery.text: When you look away, the unfatigued green cones dominate, producing the complementary color as an afterimage.

twist.text: This supports opponent process theory: color vision works in opposing pairs—red/green, blue/yellow, black/white.

climax.text: Surgeons wear green scrubs precisely to reduce red afterimages from staring at blood during long operations.

punchline.text: Green scrubs exist because of how your color neurons tire.

quiz.question: Why do afterimages show complementary colors?
options: Cone cells for the original color fatigue

details.summary: Afterimages occur when you stare at a color and then look away, seeing the complementary color. Prolonged stimulation fatigues the cone cells responsible for that color, so when you shift your gaze, the unstimulated cones dominate, producing the opposite hue.
details.whyItMatters: Afterimages reveal the opponent-process nature of color vision, where the brain processes colors in opposing pairs rather than independently.
takeaways: Staring at a color fatigues the responsive cone cells
The complementary color appears when you look away

faq.question: Why are afterimages the complementary color?
faq.answer: Color is processed in opponent pairs: red versus green, blue versus yellow. Prolonged exposure adapts one side of the pair. When the stimulus is removed, the opposing side is relatively more active, producing the complementary color.

faq.question: How long do afterimages typically last?
faq.answer: Negative afterimages from bright stimuli typically last a few seconds to a minute. Longer or brighter exposure produces longer afterimages. Very intense light sources like camera flashes can produce afterimages lasting several minutes as photoreceptors recover from the strong stimulation.
